results.result: AIB interneurons are 'rich-club' neurons with a stereotyped architecture where a single neurite is precisely placed along distinct layers of the C. elegans nerve ring neuropil. The proximal segment is positioned in the posterior neighborhood (enriched in postsynaptic specializations) and the distal segment in the anterior neighborhood (enriched in presynaptic specializations), with a posterior-anterior shift at the dorsal midline. This architecture enables AIB to receive sensory inputs from one neighborhood and relay information to the other, linking functionally distinct layers. The architecture is stereotyped across animals and developmental stages, evolutionarily conserved in nematodes, and reminiscent of amacrine cells in the vertebrate retina.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C20-C25, C91-C98 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including EM reconstructions (Figure 1), confocal imaging (Figure 1), connectomic analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and citations to published research. The data consistently demonstrate the stereotyped placement of AIB neurites in distinct neighborhoods with specific synaptic polarity, and the functional significance of this architecture for linking distinct layers. The comparisons to amacrine cells and evolutionary conservation are supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: AIB neurite placement into neighborhoods occurs during embryogenesis via a novel mechanism of retrograde zippering. The AIB neurites enter the nerve ring at ~400 m.p.f., circumnavigate the ring along the posterior neighborhood, and meet at the dorsal midline. Instead of shifting to the anterior neighborhood at the midline, they continue growing along the posterior neighborhood. At ~505 m.p.f., each AIB neurite separates from the posterior neighborhood by growing tangentially (straight outgrowth), cuts orthogonally through the nerve ring, and reengages with the arc upon intersecting the anterior neighborhood. The entire shaft of the distal AIB neurite is then peeled away from the posterior neighborhood and repositioned onto the anterior neighborhood via retrograde zippering, starting from the tip and progressively moving towards the cell body. Zippering stops at the dorsal midline (~545 m.p.f.), resulting in the adult AIB architecture. This retrograde zippering mechanism had not been previously documented in vivo during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C43, C7, C103-C104 are strongly supported by novel imaging data using diSPIM and triple-view line-scanning confocal microscopy (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The time-lapse imaging provides direct visualization of the developmental dynamics, and quantitative measurements (C37, C39) support the progressive nature of the zippering process. The claim that this mechanism had not been previously documented in vivo (C43, C102) is supported by citations to prior work showing zippering only in tissue culture (C44, C101). The straight outgrowth hypothesis (C34) is appropriately presented as speculation based on prior work (Katz, 1985).

results.result: Biophysical modeling of AIB developmental dynamics is consistent with differential adhesion mechanisms driving retrograde zippering. Zippering and unzippering occur concurrently, with similar lengths of neurite placed in the anterior neighborhood (4.49 μm) and unzippered from the posterior neighborhood (4.13 μm) between 505-545 m.p.f. Zippering velocity increases over time (from 0.09 μm/min at 515 min to 0.34 μm/min at 530 min), consistent with a net increase in adhesive forces in the anterior neighborhood. Zippering stops at the dorsal midline, likely due to balancing of adhesion and tension forces. The developmental dynamics are consistent with relative changes in adhesive forces between neighborhoods and suggest that differential adhesion mechanisms govern AIB neurite repositioning by a process similar to affinity-based sorting of cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C46-C47, C49-C54, C105-C107 are supported by quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and biophysical modeling (Appendix 1). The measurements of zippering/unzippering lengths and velocities are consistent with the proposed differential adhesion model. The interpretation that increased velocity indicates force imbalance (C50) is reasonable based on biophysical principles. The hypothesis that differential adhesion governs repositioning (C53) is appropriately presented as speculation based on the data and citations to prior work (Steinberg, 1963; Steinberg, 1970). The stopping at the dorsal midline (C51, C106) is presented as a hypothesis, which is appropriate given the data.

results.result: Loss-of-function mutant alleles of syg-1 and syg-2, which encode a pair of interacting IgCAM cell adhesion molecules, display significant defects in AIB neurite placement specifically in the anterior neighborhood. In wild type animals, complete overlap is observed between the AIB distal neurite and neurons in the anterior neighborhood. In contrast, 76.3% of syg-1(ky652) and 60% of syg-2(ky671) animals show regions of AIB detachment from the anterior neighborhood, with 20.9±3.9% and 18.6%±4.0% of the neurite segment detached, respectively. A double mutant did not enhance the defects compared to single mutants, consistent with SYG-1 and SYG-2 acting jointly. SYG-2 expression in AIB was sufficient to rescue the defects, suggesting cell-autonomous action. Expression of wild-type SYG-1 via a cosmid rescued AIB neurite placement, while AIB-specific expression did not, consistent with SYG-1 regulating AIB neurite placement cell non-autonomously.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C66 are well-supported by genetic analysis including forward and reverse genetic screens, quantitative phenotypic analysis (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and cell-specific rescue experiments (Figure 4N). The statistical analysis shows significant differences between wild type and mutants (p<0.0001, p=0.0095), with appropriate effect size estimates (d=1.087, d=0.775). The double mutant analysis (C63) supports the hypothesis that SYG-1 and SYG-2 act jointly. The rescue experiments (C64-C66) provide strong evidence for the site of action of each molecule. The characterization of SYG-1 and SYG-2 as IgCAMs (C60-C62) is supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: SYG-1 expression is dynamically regulated during embryogenesis in a pattern that coincides with AIB neurite relocation. In postembryonic larvae, syg-1 is expressed in ~20 neurons in the AIB posterior and anterior neighborhoods, with enrichment in the anterior neighborhood. Prior to 470 m.p.f., syg-1 expression is primarily restricted to the posterior neighborhood. Over the subsequent three hours (470-650 m.p.f.), SYG-1 expression levels progressively increase in the anterior neighborhood while decreasing in the posterior neighborhood, coinciding with AIB neurite relocation via retrograde zippering. Single-cell lineaging identified six neurons in the anterior neighborhood and 10 in the posterior neighborhood expressing syg-1 at ~430 m.p.f. Transcriptomic studies demonstrate a ten-fold increase in SYG-2 transcript levels in AIB during neurite transition. Increases in SYG-1 in the anterior neighborhood are caused by ingrowth of SYG-1-expressing neurons (including RIM) and onset of syg-1 expression in anterior neighborhood neurons. RIM ablations result in defects in AIB neurite placement that phenocopy syg-1 loss-of-function mutants, and expression of SYG-1 specifically in RIM and RIC neurons in syg-1 mutants was sufficient to position the AIB distal neurite along these neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C80 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence including transcriptional and translational reporter expression (Figure 5A-R'), single-cell lineaging (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), transcriptomic data (Packer et al., 2019), and genetic ablation/rescue experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 4). The temporal correlation between SYG-1 expression dynamics and AIB zippering (C71, Figure 5S) is well-documented. The RIM ablation experiments (C79) show significant defects (p<0.0001) with appropriate effect sizes (d=2.313, d=1.19), and the rescue experiments (C80) provide strong evidence for the role of SYG-1 in RIM. The hypothesis that spatiotemporal changes in SYG-1 and SYG-2 expression drive differential adhesion (C75) is appropriately presented as speculation based on the data.

results.result: Ectopic syg-1 expression in the posterior neighborhood results in a gain-of-function phenotype where the AIB distal neurite remains partially positioned in the posterior neighborhood throughout postembryonic larval stages. These gain-of-function effects are not observed in a syg-2 mutant background, consistent with SYG-2 expression in AIB being required for repositioning to SYG-1 expressing layers. Expression of the SYG-1 ectodomain in the posterior neighborhood resulted in similar gain-of-function phenotypes (although with lower penetrance), while ectopic expression of the SYG-1 endodomain did not result in mislocalization of AIB. These findings indicate that inverting the adhesion differential via enrichment of SYG-1 in the 'wrong' neighborhood predictably affects relocation of the AIB distal neurite in a way consistent with differential adhesion mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 are well-supported by ectopic expression experiments (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The gain-of-function phenotypes are quantified with significant differences (p=0.0002, p<0.0001) and appropriate effect sizes (d=1.075, d=1.140). The requirement for SYG-2 (C82) is demonstrated by the absence of gain-of-function effects in syg-2 mutants (p<0.0001). The ectodomain vs. endodomain experiments (C84-C85) provide strong evidence for the importance of adhesion-based mechanisms. The conclusion that these findings are consistent with differential adhesion mechanisms (C83) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Presynaptic proteins populate the AIB neurite in a retrograde pattern reminiscent of retrograde zippering, starting from the tip toward the dorsal midline. The timing of presynaptic site formation suggests that synaptogenesis closely follows retrograde zippering. A novel syd-2 allele exhibits synaptic defects but not AIB neurite placement defects, indicating that synaptogenesis occurs after retrograde zippering. In syg-1 mutants, RAB-3 signal is specifically reduced in regions of the AIB distal neurite incapable of repositioning to the anterior neighborhood. Ablation of RIM neurons results in defects in AIB placement in the anterior neighborhood. These findings indicate that differential adhesion regulates neurite placement via retrograde zippering, which in turn influences synaptic specificity onto target neurons. SYG-1 and SYG-2 coordinate developmental processes that result in synaptic specificity for AIB interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90, C115-C122 are supported by time-lapse imaging of presynaptic proteins (Figure 7A-K, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), genetic analysis of syd-2 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G-K), and analysis of RAB-3 localization in syg-1 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 3). The temporal relationship between zippering and synaptogenesis (C87) is well-documented. The syd-2 mutant analysis (C88) provides strong evidence that synaptogenesis and neurite placement are separable processes. The RAB-3 reduction in detached regions (C89) is statistically significant (p=0.0003) with a large effect size (d=1.643). The RIM ablation experiments (C121) are consistent with the hypothesis that postsynaptic partners contribute to AIB placement. The hypotheses about coordinated assembly of synaptic sites (C119-C120, C122) are appropriately presented as speculation based on the data.

results.result: Placement of the AVE neurite in the S2/S3 neighborhood is affected in syg-1 mutants. In wild type animals, the proximal AVE neurite runs along the RIM neurite. In syg-1 mutants, the AVE proximal neurite frequently deviates from its trajectory along RIM (50% of syg-1 mutants vs. 9.1% in wild type). The dorsal midline shift of AVE is also affected in syg-1 mutants (mean length = 2.73 μm in syg-1 vs. 3.99 μm in wild type). The detachment of the AVE neurite resembles defects that would arise from defective zippering onto the S2/S3 neighborhood. Together with the AIB studies, these observations are consistent with SYG-1 expression in a specific neuropil neighborhood resulting in specific sorting of neurites into the neighborhood by zippering mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C136 are supported by confocal imaging and quantitative analysis of AVE neurite placement in wild type and syg-1 mutants (Figure 8). The statistical analysis shows significant differences for both detachment (p=0.002, d=1.002) and dorsal midline shift length (p=0.0001, d=1.003). The interpretation that the AVE phenotype resembles defective zippering (C135) is reasonable based on the AIB data. The conclusion that SYG-1 expression results in specific sorting of neurites by zippering mechanisms (C136) is well-supported by the combined AIB and AVE data.

results.result: Differential adhesion mechanisms control precise placement of single neurites onto specific layers in the C. elegans nerve ring. Differential adhesion is orchestrated via developmentally regulated expression of the IgCAM SYG-1 and its partner ligand SYG-2. Changes in SYG-1 expression across neuropil layers result in changes in adhesive forces, which sort SYG-2-expressing neurons. Retrograde zippering depends on differential adhesion across layers and is instructed in part by the dynamic expression of SYG-1 and its interaction with SYG-2-expressing AIB neurons. While SYG-1 and SYG-2 are important for AIB neurite placement, other adhesion molecules likely act redundantly. Differences in expression levels of IgCAMs such as SYG-1 can result in differential adhesion across whole neuropils. The observed role of SYG-1 is reminiscent of its mammalian orthologs (Kirrel2/3) in axon sorting in the olfactory system and Drosophila orthologs (Hibris/Roughest) in tissue morphogenesis. Similar biophysical principles of differential adhesion might help organize neurite placement within heterogeneous tissues such as neuropils in nervous systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C8, C99, C108-C114 represent the major conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the combined evidence from imaging, biophysical modeling, genetic analysis, and ectopic expression experiments. The role of SYG-1 and SYG-2 in differential adhesion is demonstrated by multiple lines of evidence including loss-of-function mutants, rescue experiments, and gain-of-function phenotypes. The hypothesis that other adhesion molecules act redundantly (C109) is appropriately presented as speculation to explain the partial penetrance of phenotypes. The comparisons to mammalian and Drosophila orthologs (C111-C113) are supported by appropriate citations. The broader conclusion about biophysical principles organizing neurite placement (C114) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: Placement of neurites into specific neighborhoods results in laminar organization of neuropils in both vertebrates and invertebrates. This laminar organization segregates specific information streams and is a major determinant of synaptic specificity and circuit connectivity. Precise placement of neurites within layered structures cannot be exclusively explained by canonical tip-directed outgrowth dynamics. Instead, ordered placement appears to occur via local cell-cell recognition events modulated by regulated expression of specific cell adhesion molecules (CAMs). Studies in mouse and fly visual systems have revealed important roles for regulated spatio-temporal expression of IgSF proteins in targeting synaptic partner neurons to distinct layers. In C. elegans nerve bundles, neurite position is established and maintained via combinatorial, cell-specific expression of CAMs. Differential expression of CAMs in early embryos can drive compartmentalization via biophysical principles of cell adhesion and surface tension. Morphogenic developmental processes such as patterning of the Drosophila germline and retina, germ layer organization in zebrafish, and sorting of motor neuron cell bodies can be largely explained via differential adhesion mechanisms. Differential expression of N-cadherin in the Drosophila visual system underlies the organization of synaptic-partnered neurites.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C19 provide important background and context for the study and are supported by extensive citations to published research. These claims establish the broader significance of the work by placing it in the context of known mechanisms of neurite placement and differential adhesion in various systems. The citations are appropriate and support the claims made.

results.result: Other 'rich-club' neurons such as AVE and RIB are also placed along SYG-1-expressing nerve ring layers, suggesting that similar SYG-1-dependent mechanisms could underpin placement of these neurons. Zippering mechanisms via affinity-mediated adhesion might help instruct neighborhood coherence while preserving 'fluid' or transient interactions among neurites within neuropil structures. Analysis of connectome data revealed that contact profiles for single neurons vary across animals, indicative of fluid or transient interactions during development. Yet neuropils have a stereotyped and layered architecture encompassing specific circuits. Dynamic expression of adhesion molecules might help preserve tissue organization in tangled neuropils via the creation of affinity relationships of relative strengths. These relationships would contribute to the sorting of neurites onto specific strata through biophysical interactions occurring via differential adhesion. Spatiotemporally restricted expression of CAMs in layers would result in dynamic, affinity-mediated relationships that preserve neighborhood coherence in the context of 'fluid' or transient interactions among neurites.
results.evaluation: Claims C100, C123-C129 represent speculative hypotheses about the broader implications of the findings. While the observation that AVE and RIB are placed along SYG-1-expressing layers (C100) is supported by data, the suggestion that similar mechanisms underpin their placement is speculative. The hypotheses about zippering mechanisms preserving neighborhood coherence while allowing fluid interactions (C123-C129) are interesting and plausible based on the data and connectome analysis (C124), but require additional experimental validation. These claims are appropriately presented as speculation in the manuscript.
